problems.description: 13 naming violations across 5 files (celery_config.py, notifications.py, repositories.py, test_app.py, app.py): classes not PascalCase, functions not snake_case, module-level constants not UPPER_CASE — convention score 0.69. New modules were added without following the established naming scheme.

Scope creep in a single feature session: +33 functions, +16 imports, +2 files (celery_config.py, notifications.py, repositories.py) introduce multiple new subsystems (background workers, notifications, repository layer) at once, risking half-wired infrastructure that the existing tests/app.py may not exercise.

Moving from DB-backed tokens to stateless HS256 JWT removes server-side token revocation; worse, SECRET_KEY defaults to a random per-boot value, so all tokens are silently invalidated on every restart unless SECRET_KEY is set in the environment.
f-string interpolated SQL in _migrate_legacy_schema (even though {owner_col} is drawn from a fixed set, building SQL via f-string is an injection-adjacent smell that static tools flag).
Cognitive complexity +11 concentrated in _migrate_legacy_schema and verify_password/_is_legacy_hash branching; the migration helper would benefit from splitting table-migration into per-table steps.
get_user_from_token swallows all JWT/KeyError/TypeError errors into a bare 'return None', masking the failure reason and providing no clock-skew tolerance for token exp.

strengths: Stateless JWT auth with proper sub/iat/exp payload replacing the custom DB token table.
Real password hashing via werkzeug generate_password_hash with a lazy, idempotent upgrade path for legacy static-salt sha256 hashes on successful login.
_migrate_legacy_schema is repeat-safe, never drops user or task rows, and handles both user_id/owner_id column naming — well-designed migration for items→tasks rename.
Dead code removed (verify_token wrapper) and SonarQube smells down -4, bugs +0.
commit_reviews.summary: A security-positive feature session that correctly moves to JWT + werkzeug hashing with a safe idempotent migration, but pays for it with a low convention score (0.69, 13 naming violations in 5 files) and over-broad scope (+33 functions, +16 imports) that adds technical debt.

problems.description: New celery_config.py and notifications.py define module-level constants in lowercase (broker_url, result_backend, task_routes, celery_app) where the framework convention requires UPPER_CASE — this drives much of the 0.69 score. Flagged discrepancy: lowercase config is the standard Celery idiom, so the mechanical checker partially penalizes an intentional pattern.

PascalCase violations reported in app.py, test_app.py, and repositories.py predate this commit — the AST diff adds +0 classes, so the 0.69 convention score over-counts pre-existing violations when attributed to this diff.
Migration backfills fabricated emails via `username || '@example.com'`, injecting synthetic data into a real column; acceptable for a mocked notification story but worth a comment or config flag.
update_task reads `user["email"]` from the auth-loaded user dict; safe only because the migration guarantees the column, but a missing-key guard would harden it against older sessions.
SonarQube delta (+1 smell, cognitive complexity +7) is modest and stems mostly from the completion-detection branch in update_task; no structural concern.

strengths: New PUT /tasks/{id} endpoint enforces ownership via owner_id in the WHERE clause and reuses the existing @require_auth decorator, matching the codebase's route security pattern.
_migrate_add_columns mirrors the existing _migrate_legacy_schema pattern and is idempotent (PRAGMA table_info guard) for pre-existing databases.
Thorough test coverage for the new endpoint: success, 404, 401, cross-user ownership, and default status — no new bugs, zero duplication.
Async notification via Celery .delay() keeps the request path non-blocking and correctly fires only on a pending→completed transition.
Backwards-compatible schema evolution with NOT NULL DEFAULT'' / DEFAULT 'pending' keeps existing rows valid.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-tested integration commit that extends the task API with an owned-scoped update endpoint and async notification while faithfully following the app's existing decorator/migration/test conventions — the 0.69 convention score mostly reflects intentional Celery lowercase config plus pre-existing violations, not this diff's own work.

problems.description: Repository singletons (user_repo, task_repo) are instantiated at module import time in app.py, coupling object lifecycle to import order rather than the Flask app context.
The legacy-hash upgrade-on-login logic remains business logic in the route handler (app.py login) rather than being owned by the UserRepository, so the extraction is incomplete for auth concerns.
Introduces a new repository abstraction layer where none existed in the codebase; consistent within this commit, but it sets a pattern future handlers must follow.
Cognitive complexity +2 despite the refactor (per SonarQube delta); the long login handler and update_task branching are the likely contributors and could have been simplified further.

strengths: Eliminates repeated `with get_db() as conn:` SQL boilerplate across all user and task CRUD endpoints into dedicated repository classes.
Extraction is consistent and complete: register, login, list/create/get/update/delete tasks all migrated to repositories.py.
Preserves the owner-scoping authorization predicates (find_by_id_and_owner) — no security semantics changed.
SonarQube delta confirms zero new bugs, zero new smells, and zero new duplications.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, consistent repository-pattern extraction that reduces duplicated SQL and handler boilerplate with no new bugs or smells; the low 0.69 convention score reflects largely pre-existing violations (celery_config.py, notifications.py, test_app.py) not introduced by this diff — a discrepancy worth noting, since the new code itself (PascalCase TaskRepository/UserRepository) is convention-compliant.

compounding_issues: Session 1 (greenfield) shipped zero code: it spent the whole session asking about a seed contradiction (SQLite vs 'flat files, no databases') and the question was never actually resolved — Session 2 silently picked SQLite and moved on, so the session produced no value.

Legacy-compatibility debt locked in at Session 2 and never paid down: the seed's pre-JWT `tokens`/`items` schema forced permanent `_is_legacy_hash` sha256 verification, lazy password-upgrade logic, and `_migrate_legacy_schema`/`_migrate_add_columns` that still ship in HEAD (app.py:68-109, 122-131) even though the legacy seed was never deployed anywhere.

Growing hard Redis coupling: Session 3 (Celery broker) and Session 5 (Flask-Limiter storage) both hardcode redis://localhost:6379; a down broker silently degrades notifications and rate limiting falls back to in-memory with warnings — a runtime dependency never surfaced or handled.
rate_limit_key() calls get_user_from_token on every authenticated request, adding a per-request DB hit inside the rate-limit path — a minor but compounding performance smell as traffic scales.
key_decisions: Session 2 replaced the seed's custom stateless token auth with PyJWT + werkzeug password hashing, preserving data via a backward-compatible migration — the most consequential choice, since every later session keys off the JWT user identity (ownership scoping, per-user rate limits).
Session 3 added async completion notifications as a Celery task invoked via `.delay()` and mocked in tests, so the suite needs no live broker — kept integration testable without infrastructure.

Session 4 extracted a repository/DAO layer (BaseRepository ABC + TaskRepository/UserRepository), which made Session 5's pagination an additive one-file change instead of a rewrite — the refactor paid off immediately.
Session 5 added Redis-backed per-user rate limiting (Flask-Limiter) and cursor-based pagination, and removed the now-unused find_by_owner — disciplined feature work paired with cleanup.
Session 1's halt-and-clarify instead of guessing on the contradictory storage spec avoided a wrong-footed implementation, though no code landed.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality rose monotonically across sessions: the test suite grew 22 → 33 → 33 → 52 and stayed green before every commit, and each session fully realized its intent (JWT hardening, async notifications, repository refactor, rate limiting + pagination). The clearest improvement came in Session 4's refactor, which made Session 5's cross-cutting work mostly additive and localized, and the code at HEAD is clean, typed, and documented. The only blemishes are the permanent legacy-migration/sha256-compatibility code carried from Session 2 and the zero-code greenfield session.
story_review.summary: A coherent, well-tested five-session arc that improved steadily — JWT auth hardening, Celery notifications, a clean repository-layer refactor, then per-user rate limiting and pagination — marred only by a zero-code greenfield session and permanently carried legacy-migration debt.
